motion: Does the evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism?

routes.description: A cumulative Christian-theist route arguing that cosmological origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and personal religious experience jointly favor the Christian God over skeptical atheism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited evidence is established, its principal naturalistic alternatives are inadequate, and its combined explanatory force makes the specifically Christian God more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

bridges.description: The evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.
The cumulative convergence of the five evidential lines supplies good reason to accept Christian theism and no comparably good reason to accept atheism.
The universe's finite beginning and need for a cause imply an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial transcendent cause.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
The empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by God raising Jesus from the dead.

routes.description: A skeptical-atheist route arguing that the proposed evidence is uncertain, underdetermines the Christian God, admits natural alternatives, and conflicts with what would be expected from an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect being.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal theistic inferences lack adequate evidential support or specificity and the observed world is at least as expected under skeptical atheism as under the Christian God hypothesis.

bridges.description: The cited evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism and instead supports withholding or rejecting belief in the Christian God.
The five proposed evidential lines fail to meet the strong burden required for the specific Christian God hypothesis because their inferences are underdetermined and face contrary empirical evidence.
The Kalam inference is inadequately supported because ordinary causal experience does not establish causation for creation ex nihilo or for the physical universe as a whole.
Fine-tuning probabilities are epistemically uncertain, admit deeper physical or multiverse explanations, and do not identify an omniperfect Christian God.
The world's evil and opaque divine presence are empirically less expected from a morally perfect Christian God than from skeptical atheism.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, it has a transcendent cause whose relation to time, space, and the causal regress requires it to be uncaused, timeless, changeless, spaceless, and immaterial.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A transcendent nonphysical cause must be an unembodied mind because the only alternative candidate, an abstract object, cannot stand in causal relations; therefore the universe has a personal creator.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Life-permitting fine-tuning is extraordinarily improbable under chance, is not physically necessary, exhibits an independent pattern, and therefore is best explained by design.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values are evident in moral experience and, because they require God as their ground, their existence entails God's existence.
moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus' empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and the disciples' unexpected resurrection belief lack a plausible naturalistic explanation and are best explained by God raising Jesus, thereby evidencing God's existence.
moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A sincere seeker can know that God exists apart from argument through immediate personal experience, in which God is encountered as a directly given reality rather than merely adopted as an idea.
moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Because mutually incompatible religions are acquired and maintained through similar sources such as upbringing, preaching, sacred texts, and religious experience, those methods are unreliable guides to truth.
moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even generously allowing disembodied mentality some prior probability, the specific omniperfect Christian God must compete with thousands of conflicting religious hypotheses, so absent an overwhelmingly strong case the rational conclusion is disbelief or at least agnosticism.
moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Ordinary causal experience concerns rearrangements of existing material and therefore does not justify extending the premise that whatever begins to exist has a cause to creation from nothing.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes only a beginning to expansion, while contracting models and unresolved quantum-gravity problems prevent confidence in an absolute cosmic beginning.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: There is no evidence that minds exist without physical substrates, and even if the universe had a nonphysical cause it need not be an abstract object or mind but could be a kind of cause beyond evolved human comprehension.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Religious disagreement does not discredit one common belief-forming method because religions do not share a single method, while Craig's own case uses logic, evidence, and personal experience.
moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem still implies an absolute cosmic beginning, is independent of Einstein's gravitational equations and any quantum-gravity description, and therefore supplies strong cosmological evidence that the universe began.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The absence of observed creation from nothing does not undermine causation, because originating without either material or efficient cause would be still more absurd than originating without a material cause alone.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: If the fundamental constants were shown to be physically inexplicable and precisely selected from a broad range of alternatives, that coincidence would naturally invite explanation by a cosmic designer.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning warrants caution because humans readily over-detect purpose, cosmic probability judgments rest on one observed universe, deeper physics may explain the constants, and a multiverse would make life-permitting observation unsurprising.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even established cosmic fine-tuning would not identify the morally perfect Christian God because the same life-enabling conditions are equally compatible with an evil or morally neutral designer.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The nonunique result of subtracting infinity from infinity is not a contradiction but merely reflects that the inverse equation has multiple solutions, just as division of zero by zero is undefined without making zero incoherent.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Absence of evidence counts against God only if God's existence would make substantially more evidence probable, and Millican has supplied no grounds for that expectation beyond personal opinion.
moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Millican's admission that infinite subtraction lacks a unique value is precisely the problem for a real collection, because physically removing equal infinite quantities from equal totals should not yield unequal remainders.
moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning probabilities can be assessed by comparing possible parameter ranges with the narrow life-permitting range, diverse cases are unlikely all to disappear under future physics, and moral character is supplied by Craig's separate moral argument.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An atheist can apprehend objective moral values without knowing their ultimate nature, and neither objective morality nor intrinsic human value evidently depends on God's existence.
moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The resurrection reports are late, non-eyewitness Christian advocacy documents; Matthew and Luke depend on Mark and another common source, and the accounts contain chronological and theological discrepancies, so they provide weak evidence for God.
moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Naturalism supplies no nonarbitrary basis for privileging human or sentient flourishing and cannot explain binding moral obligations without a moral lawgiver.
moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The three facts used in Craig's resurrection inference are accepted by a majority of historians, and even Millican's cited skeptical scholars accept the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief.
moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The observed world's evil and purported divine morality do not match expectations for a perfect God, so the evidence favors skepticism and provides strong evidence against God's existence with very little in favor.
moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning and Craig's other presented arguments do not establish infinite power; at most they infer a being of enormous power, while an additional ontological argument would be needed for infinity.
moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Natural and moral evil may be permitted because God's purpose is to bring people freely into an eternal relationship with him, and an evil-containing world may maximize those who freely do so.
moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
